newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to touch on medium-term plan in IMF talks.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to touch on medium-term plan in IMF talks.

text.p: Turkey will mention the outlines of a medium-term stability programme being drafted by the government to a visiting team from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), State Minister Ufuk Soylemez said on Wednesday.
"We are preparing a medium-term stability programme. We will discuss its principles with the IMF team," he told reporters in Ankara.

"I will explain the details of the programme to the IMF when I go to the governors' meeting in Washington towards the end of April. But before that we as the government should draw up the details," he said.
The programme, expected to cover three years from its implementation, aims at lowering annual inflation to single digits from its current level of 79 percent, and narrow public deficits.
It is expected to include measures to improve social security system, one of the major holes draining state funds, and speed up other structural reforms including privatisation.

The IMF team, who arrived in Istanbul on Tuesday, are scheduled to meet businessmen in there and later proceed to Ankara to hold talks with top economy officials during their two-week-long consultation visit under IMF's Article Four.

Soylemez, in charge of treasury and privatisation in the coalition government between Islamists and conservatives, joined other Turkish officials in ruling out a stand-by accord, recommended by the business community.
"The IMF has come to Turkey for about 40 years and we signed only 16 stand-by agreements with them. We should not expect a stand-by deal after each visit of the IMF," he said.
"We will show them the positive developments in the first quarter of 1997 and good performance of our economy compared to the first quarter of 1996," he said.
He said Turkey was doing better in the first quarter compared to previous year in terms of privatisation, struggle with inflation and foreign currency reserves.
He said Turkey had recently approved privatisations worth about $800 million and managed to raise central bank reserves to $16 billion now from $12 billion in the first quarter of 1996.

He did not give details on the full contents of the talks with the IMF, which last visited Turkey in October, but said: "We will ask the IMF to continue its international credit support for Turkey during talks."
Turkish markets and political leaders are looking to the IMF's visit for some support for the government's economic policies.
But economists, businessmen and even some officials say the team will find their interlocutors hamstrung by political concerns and unable to address the Fund's desires for structural reform.

Turkey's year-on-year inflation was running at 78.6 percent in February, a level it has held since 1984. Public sector borrowing totals over eight percent of GNP, compared with the 12 percent that helped touch off a financial crisis in April of that same year.
Economists predict Turkey's ambitious balanced budget target for 1997 after a 1,217-trillion lira deficit last year would not be welcomed by the IMF.
